notes: Surfnerd overview: Kaena Point is the westernmost tip of Oahu, a torrential convergence zone where North and South Pacific swell energy collides with spectacular force. It breaks over reef and rock, with lava and coral in the mix, and throws both rights and lefts as a reef and point setup. On the big N or NW swells that light it up, it stacks giant righthanders around the west side of the island and careens them down along the southern edge of the headland. Further down the point sits Yokohama Bay, where the waves run a touch tamer but can still reach serious, heavy proportions. This is expert-only terrain. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. notes: Surfnerd overview: Lopa Beach is a long, white-sand beach on the east coast of Lanai, with a stretch of reef just offshore that serves up a variety of peaks and sections. The reef breaks both right and left over lava, rock, and coral, and there's enough on offer for surfers of every ability. It's a pristine setting, though this rates as a below-average spot overall: it can get genuinely fun when swell and wind line up, but that combination doesn't come together all that often. Skill (surfnerd): Beginner, Intermediate, Expert. Access (surfnerd): Getting here takes some effort: Lopa Beach is only reachable via 4X4-only dirt roads that branch off Keomuku Road, so a regular vehicle won't cut it. Mind the reef beneath you.

notes: Surfnerd overview: Majors Bay is a powerful, exposed break on the long, empty west coast of Kauai. It faces open ocean and pulls in energy from both the North and South Pacific, so there's swell potential across autumn, winter, spring, and summer. The surf here is all about rights, and the whole stretch is known for serious power and terrifying rips, where a single long ride can turn into a long walk back down the beach. Strong currents and the chance of sharks come with the territory. Check: surfnerd states facing WSW but best swell N (112.5 degrees apart); both are as published. Skill (surfnerd): Expert. Surf-forecast Majors-Bay: "Majors Bay in Kauai is an exposed beach and point break that has quite consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. Works best in offshore winds from the northeast. Tends to receive distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south. The beach breaks offers right-handers When it's working here, it can get crowded. Dangerous rips are a hazard of surfing here." Access (surfnerd): Getting to the water is easy: pull off the road, walk onto the beach almost anywhere, find a good peak, and paddle out. The standout north-swell right runs down the reef at the end of the runway, though, and that one sits on the military missile range and needs an access pass. Paddles can be short and quick when it's small, and long and tiring when it's big and consistent. The water is pristine most of the time, turning murky only after heavy rains push farmland runoff into the lineup. Other guide pins from this position: surf-forecast Majors-Bay 2.1 km.

It comes with a price, though: heavy rips, uneven bottom contours, littoral currents, undertows, and a nasty shorepound, so it's realistically a summer or tiny-swell spot rather than a year-round one.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Ventura Overhead is the standout at Emma Wood State Beach, where the coast bends between Ventura and the points and reefs beyond. It is a famous big-wave break that once served as training grounds for California's big-wave pioneers, and it still ranks as the area's premier big-wave spot. It only breaks a few times a year, but when it does it throws wedgy, open-face rights that funnel for hundreds of yards, along with steep, lined-up lefts that can barrel when there is enough west in the swell.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Cape Lookout sits behind the longest cape on the West Coast, and that headland shapes everything about the place. The water is about the cleanest and clearest in Oregon, and it stays a beautiful spot to visit whether or not it's breaking. It was once known for a quality righthand reef, locally called Boy Scout Camp, but geological upheaval wrecked that wave, and today the surf is mostly beachbreak with both lefts and rights.

guideSummary.surfForecast: There are two point/river mouth breaks at Twin Rivers . The best swell direction is west to northwest. The left is the most surfed break off the western river, it is malibu going left. The wave is soft with easy drop-ins and can hold a big swell with rippable forgiving long walls. S-SE offshore winds are best for this break which works at low to mid tide. The right is less surfed and breaks off the east river. guideSummary.surfnerd:
Overview

7th Street is a sand-bottomed beach and jetty break in Ocean City, and when it's on it arguably serves up the best left in town. Rights and lefts both break here: swells jack up off the 7th Street jetty, throwing out farther than they are high, then wall up and peel off more sanely down the rest of the beach. It shows its full potential from head-high to double-overhead, with big lefts rolling off the north jetty during a nor'easter and a decent right off the south jetty on a good southerly swell.

Two deep-water peaks define the spot: the lefts run as long, workable walls, while K39's more eastern take-off offers shorter, steeper rights. Don't expect barrels here, even when it's as big as it gets, which is part of why it's a favorite for longboarders and cruisers.

It is not especially hollow, but it is fast and racy, and it can barrel toward the inside on bigger days.

The sandbar break provides left and right handers. When it's working here, it can get crowded.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Pools is a white sandy beach on the Punta side of Rincon, right where you come down the hill, and it hides a few shifty reef peaks rather than the sand you might expect. The beach sits somewhat protected from the northeast trades, and the peaks break over shallow rock, occasionally throwing a barrel. It's not really a destination spot and stays fairly average by Rincon standards, but it makes for a fun, quiet morning session.

guideSummary.surfnerd: San Juan is a quality lefthander sitting just east of La Santa, breaking over a large reef that is thick with sea urchins. The wave sets up well outside, and when everything lines up it produces genuinely classic surf. It is not a forgiving setup, though: the shallow inside section can suck dry as the tide drops, and getting caught inside on a big swell is an unpleasant place to be.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Sandy Beach is a fickle but rewarding left that peels off a rocky outcropping in Puerto Rico, breaking over a combination of uneven reef and sand. When the sand banks up over the reef and the wind cooperates, it can get really good, turning round and hollow through the inside once it hits a few feet overhead. It is essentially a one-peak wave, so the action concentrates in a single spot.

Several peaks spread across the reef, giving a big playing field and plenty of room to find your own wave. Expect anything from fun shoulders to punchy barrels depending on how the swell lines up.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Table Top is a serious right-hand reef barrel on Puerto Rico's northwest corner, just north of Surfer's Beach and one of the first waves you reach coming around the point. It takes its name from the flat, exposed slab of reef that looks like a table, with the barrel spinning round right in front of the cliff over live coral. This is an expert-only wave: shallow, slabbing and sharp, with dangerous rocks on the inside and an exposed rock platform right at the takeoff.

Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the north. There is a right breaking reef. It very rarely gets crowded here. Hazards include urchins, rips, rocks and pollution.

guideSummary.surfnerd: The Point is a right-hand reef point that breaks over rock, and technically it's the top section of Maria's rather than a break of its own. It sets up right in front of an exposed chunk of reef, and the wave is mostly a high-line wall, so you need down-the-line speed straight off the takeoff. A strong northwest swell changes that character completely: it bowls, jacks and tubes.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Tocones is a short, viciously hollow right-hander over reef that most surfers will never see break. Standing in the entry and exit channel at Aviones, look east to the shallow slab of reef throwing waves close to shore. Most days it just looks like dry rock, but on the right swell it turns into one of the most lethal little waves in Puerto Rico.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Tres Palmas is Puerto Rico's most famous big-wave break, a right-hander that peels off the last and furthest-out section of the long reef running down from Domes. A deepwater trench sits just outside, focusing long-period swell into big, meaty peaks that stand up fast and then open into long walls. Once you make the drop there's a large canvas ahead, roughly 75 yards of rumbling wall built for big, drawn-out turns rather than quick, flashy surfing.

No reef break here. Sometimes crowded. Hazards include urchins and rocks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Wilderness is a broad, sweeping reef in Aguadilla that lives up to its name, both on land and in the water. Locals call it Wildo, and plenty of surfers have had that lost-in-the-woods feeling while hunting down a shifty, double-overhead wall without getting caught inside. Small days serve up scattered little peaks with short, bowly lefts and slightly longer, more facey rights.

The best wind direction is from the east. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells A right hand reef break. Good surf at all stages of the tide. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Beware of urchins, rips and rocks.
